'''''Buddleja cordata''''' is [[endemic]] to [[Mexico]], growing along forest edges and water courses at elevations of 1500–3000 m; it has also naturalized in parts of Ethiopia.<ref name=Norman>Norman, E. M. (2000). Buddlejaceae. ''Flora Neotropica 81'', New York Botanical Garden, USA</ref><ref name=Leeuwenberg>Leeuwenberg, A. J. M. (1979) ''The Loganiaceae of Africa XVIII Buddleja L. II, Revision of the African & Asiatic species''. H. Veenman & Zonen, Wageningen, Nederland.</ref>  The species was first described and named by [[Carl Sigismund Kunth|Kunth]] in 1818.<ref name = Nova>''Nova Genera et Species Plantarum'', 2: 348–349, t.185. 1818.</ref>

==Description==
''Buddleja cordata'' is a large [[deciduous]] [[dioecious]] shrub or tree < 20 m tall in the wild. The trunk, which can reach 45 cm in diameter, has a furrowed bark, brownish or blackish in colour. The [[leaf shape|ovate to narrowly elliptical]] leaves are opposite and paired, 4–23  cm long by 3–14 cm wide, on [[petiole (botany)|petioles]] 1–4 cm long. The terminal [[inflorescence]]s are [[panicle|paniculate]], 6–30 cm long with at least two orders of branches, the lowermost subtended by leaves, the uppermost by small bracts. The small fragrant flowers are grouped into shortly [[peduncle (botany)|pedunculate]] [[cyme (botany)|cymule]]s, the [[corolla (flower)|corollas]] white, cream, or yellow, with a flush of orange at the throat, 1.5–2.5 long. [[Ploidy]]: ''2n'' = 76 (tetraploid).<ref name=Norman/>

==Cultivation==
The species is cold hardy in the [[UK]]. A large specimen grows in the Centenary Border of the [[Sir Harold Hillier Gardens]] in [[Hampshire]], another as part of the [[NCCPG]] national collection at [[Longstock Park]] Nursery, also in Hampshire.<ref name=Moore>Moore, P. (2012). ''Buddleja List 2011-2012 Longstock Park Nursery''. Longstock Park, UK.</ref> [[Hardiness zone|Hardiness]]: [[United States Department of Agriculture|USDA]] zone 8.
<ref name=Stuart>Stuart, D. (2006). ''Buddlejas''. Plant Collector Guide. Timber Press, Oregon, USA. {{ISBN|978-0-88192-688-0}}</ref>

==Uses==
The species (and the genus as a whole) contain secondary [[metabolites]] such as [[flavonoids]] and [[iridoid]] [[glycosides]] which have shown much promise in the treatment of cancers and a wide range of other disorders.<ref name=Norman/>
